identity.title: Bluetooth RC Car
identity.tagline: Drive a small robot car from your phone — no custom app, just a Bluetooth terminal.

goal: Build a two-wheeled car that's driven wirelessly from a smartphone over Bluetooth, using single-character commands (forward, back, left, right, stop) sent from any generic Bluetooth serial app — turning the Line-Following Robot's exact chassis and motor wiring into something you steer yourself instead of something that steers itself.
simpleSummary: Drive a robot car from your phone over Bluetooth, sending simple forward/back/turn commands.
howItWorks: The HC-05 module is, from the Arduino's point of view, nothing more exotic than a wireless wire: whatever character a paired phone app sends over Bluetooth shows up on the HC-05's serial output exactly as if it had been typed into the Serial Monitor, and vice versa. This project uses SoftwareSerial to create a second serial channel on two ordinary digital pins, dedicated to talking to the HC-05, so the Arduino's main USB serial connection stays free for debugging. The car itself reuses precisely the same L298N direction/speed wiring and motor-control functions as the Line-Following Robot — the only thing that changes is where the "which way to go" decision comes from: a phone's button press over Bluetooth, instead of a line sensor's reading.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
A Bluetooth serial terminal app on your phone (e.g. "Serial Bluetooth Terminal" on Android)
Small Phillips screwdriver for chassis assembly

components.note: or any 6-12V pack matching your motors

circuitDiagramCaption: HC-05 talks to the Arduino over SoftwareSerial (D10/D11); everything downstream of the Arduino is identical to the Line-Following Robot's motor wiring.

wiringSteps.instruction: Build the chassis exactly as in the Line-Following Robot: mount both motors and wheels, attach the caster wheel, and wire the motors to the L298N's OUT1/OUT2 and OUT3/OUT4.
wiringSteps.detail: If you've already built that project, this entire stage is identical — only the "brain" deciding direction changes.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire Arduino D2 → L298N IN1, D3 → IN2, D4 → IN3, D5 → IN4, D6 → ENA, D9 → ENB.
wiringSteps.detail: Same direction/speed pin pattern used throughout this encyclopedia's motor-driver projects, just on a fresh set of pin numbers to keep clear of the Bluetooth wiring.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the HC-05's TXD to Arduino D10, and RXD to Arduino D11.
wiringSteps.detail: Notice this is crossed — the module's transmit pin goes to the pin the code treats as its receive pin, and vice versa, exactly like any serial connection between two devices.

wiringSteps.instruction: Wire the HC-05's VCC to Arduino 5V and GND to GND.
wiringSteps.detail: Some HC-05 boards' RXD pin technically expects 3.3V logic and can be sensitive to the Arduino's 5V signal over long-term use — a simple voltage divider (two resistors) on that one wire is a common precaution, though many boards tolerate 5V fine in practice.

wiringSteps.instruction: Connect the battery to the L298N's +12V/GND, and connect that ground to Arduino GND.
wiringSteps.detail: The same non-negotiable shared-ground rule as every motor-driver project here.

wiringSteps.instruction: Pair your phone with the HC-05 (default pairing code is usually 1234 or 0000) and install any generic Bluetooth serial terminal app.
wiringSteps.detail: You don't need a custom app for this project — any app that sends plain text characters over a Bluetooth serial connection works, since the Arduino is just watching for single letters.

code.explanation: bluetooth.available() checks whether a new character has arrived without blocking the rest of the program while waiting — the car simply keeps doing whatever it was last told until a new command interrupts it. The switch statement is a direct lookup from received character to motor function, and every motor function itself is the same set of direction/speed writes used across every other motor-driver project in this encyclopedia — nothing about the actual driving logic is new here, only the source of the commands.

expectedBehavior: Sending F, B, L, R, or S from a Bluetooth terminal app immediately drives the car forward, backward, pivots it left or right, or stops it — continuing that action until a new command arrives.

troubleshooting.issue: Phone can't find or pair with the HC-05.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm the module has power (its LED should blink, rapidly when unpaired) and that you're searching in your phone's Bluetooth settings, not inside a specific app, for the initial pairing.

troubleshooting.issue: Commands are received (LED activity) but the car doesn't move correctly.
troubleshooting.fix: This is the same troubleshooting as any L298N-driven build — check shared ground between Arduino and L298N, and that no ENA/ENB jumper caps are left in place overriding the PWM speed control.

troubleshooting.issue: Car responds to some letters but not others.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm your terminal app is sending exactly the single uppercase characters expected (F, B, L, R, S) — some apps add extra characters like a newline that won't match the switch statement but also won't break anything, so this is usually a typo in the app's button configuration, not a code bug.

troubleshooting.issue: Bluetooth connection drops or lags noticeably.
troubleshooting.fix: Move closer — HC-05's practical range is often shorter (a few meters) than its rated range, especially indoors with walls between the phone and car.

extensions: Add a speed command (e.g. digits 1-9 sent before a direction) instead of one fixed SPEED value.
Build a simple custom phone app (e.g. with MIT App Inventor) with actual on-screen direction buttons instead of a raw text terminal.
Combine with the Obstacle-Avoidance Robot's ultrasonic sensor as a safety override that stops the car regardless of commands if it's about to hit something.
Compare this build directly against the RF433 Remote-Control Car project — same driving logic, completely different wireless link.
